extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes patentable subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, design) and how to judge whether an improvement or claimed advance qualifies as an invention under U.S. law. Includes definitions, distinctions (process vs principle), and negative rules for determining invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes recognize processes (arts), machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, and designs as the principal classes of patentable subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that processes are patentable as arts; machines are combinations of parts; some things made by hand are 'manufactures'; compositions cover two-or-more-substance composites; designs are separately patentable under Section 4929. Notes that classification among these heads is often obvious and that an inventor need not determine the precise class to obtain a valid patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a machine
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine is a combination of heterogeneous mechanical parts, adapted to receive energy and to apply it to the production of some energetic result or results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All parts of a machine may be old while the machine as a whole and its sub-combinations are proper subjects of patents (subcombinations patentable). Improvements may be additions, subtractions, substitutions, or rearrangements of parts; patentability of an improvement depends on several considerations addressed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of composition of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'composition of matter' covers all compositions of two or more substances, including composite articles resulting from chemical union or mechanical mixture, and gases, fluids, powders, or solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be a proper subject of a patent, a composition must, like other categories, endure the tests of invention, novelty, and utility discussed in subsequent chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'manufacture' (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Manufacture' in American patent law has a narrower meaning than in England; processes are patentable as arts, machines and compositions are separate categories, and anything made by hand of man that is neither machine nor composition nor design is a 'manufacture'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes possible inclusion of building structures and that exact classification is often unimportant to obtaining a patent; a seventeen-year patent may be lawfully granted for a thing which falls under either designation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent eligibility (ornamental requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent requires a new, original, and ornamental design for an article of manufacture (Section 4929, as amended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amended statute uses 'ornamental' to specify a necessary characteristic; utility is not required and its absence does not deprive patentability. However, an article ordinarily not visible in its ordinary use is not proper subject-matter for a design patent. Nor is an article patentable as a design if the essential element is a mechanical construction causing the article to assume an ornamental shape. It is questionable whether ornamentation that gives no value (e.g., certain tools) is proper subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process vs. principle distinction (laws of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a process is a patent for the described combined use of all the laws of nature utilized by that process; a patent for a principle is a patent for one only of the laws of nature used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent claims a principle (a single law of nature) it would be broader than a process patent because it would cover all processes aiming at the same result that use that law, regardless of combination. Granting patents for principles would suppress subsequent invention. Illustrations: Harley, Whitney, Tilghman, and Bell claimed combined uses (processes) and were sustained; Morse's eighth claim was construed to cover the use of electric current alone (a principle) and was overthrown. Proper drafting to claim the combined and methodical use of laws avoids this problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent for a process includes combined use of multiple laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an inventor produces a process utilizing several laws of nature, a patent claiming the entire process (including the use of all those laws in the described order and method) is a patent for a process and is allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a process claim will not cover other processes which omit one or more of the laws used by the claimed process (e.g., Bain's telegraph vs. Morse's). The practical distinction is whether the claim is confined to one law or claims the combination and methodical use of several.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements as patentable subjects (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements of machines constitute patentable subject-matter and may consist of additions, subtractions, substitutions, or rearrangements of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a given improvement is patentable depends on several considerations: it must be an 'invented' improvement (not merely produced otherwise), and whether using the improvement infringes earlier patents is treated separately. Patents are not void merely because they include old inventions; an improvement may or may not be invention and may or may not infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of invention for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are grantable for things 'invented' (the word 'discovered' in the statute has the meaning of 'invented'); novelty and utility alone are not enough—there must be invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invention is often a question of fact; a thing must be the product of some exercise of the inventive faculties to be patentable. The rule applies to processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, and designs. Intermediate steps that rise to invention are entitled to protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single affirmative test for invention; use of negative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no concise affirmative rule to determine invention in every case; courts resolve the question by applying several negative rules (rules of exclusion) that classify variations that do or do not involve invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates and will elaborate many negative rules and their exceptions; the presence or absence of the 'impalpable something' distinguishing invention from mere skill is determined case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: mere mechanical skill (ordinary artisan's work)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not invention to produce a device which any skillful mechanic, electrician, chemist, or other expert would produce when required to effectuate a given result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Bradley's classic paragraph explains that the patent laws are not intended to monopolize every slight advance that would occur to skilled workmen; granting patents for trifling devices developed by ordinary skill would obstruct invention and encourage speculative patenting. Courts apply this principle broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: excellence of workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence of workmanship or superior execution of known techniques is not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mere workmanship from exercise of inventive faculty; praised artisanship does not satisfy the statutory requirement of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: substitution of materials (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting materials is generally not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are exceptions (to be stated in later sections), but mere material substitution that does not change mode of operation or produce a non-obvious result is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: enlargement or change of degree (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply enlarging or changing the degree (scale/intensity) of an old thing is not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are recognized exceptions (e.g., where change of degree results in a new mode of operation or unexpected advantage), but as a general negative rule enlargement/change of degree is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregation — merely bringing old elements together without a new mode of operation — is not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An aggregation lacking a new cooperative or synergistic mode of operation will not qualify; contrast with a new combination that changes mode of operation (which can be invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: duplication (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplication of known devices or features is not generally invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple replication or duplication without new mode, function, or unexpected result will not satisfy the inventive requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: omission (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of elements from a known device is not generally invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing parts that do not create a new mode of operation or produce non-obvious effects will not amount to invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: substitution of equivalents (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting equivalents is not generally invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a substitution is obvious to a person skilled in the art and does not change mode of operation, it is not inventive; exceptions exist where equivalents produce unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: new combination without new mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of old elements that does not produce a new mode of operation is not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere bringing together of old elements without functional cooperation beyond their known uses will be treated as non-inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not invention: using an old thing for a new analogous purpose (generally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an old thing for a new and analogous purpose is generally not invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are cases where this rule does not apply (exceptions discussed elsewhere); whether an analogous new use involves inventive faculty depends on whether the use is non-obvious and provides new utility or function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving doubts: comparative utility test
rubrics_metrics.description: When doubts about invention are otherwise insoluble, they may be resolved by ascertaining comparative utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts can compare relative utility of the alleged invention versus prior art to decide whether the advance is inventive; this is one guide among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention is a question of fact investigated in light of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of invention are to be decided as questions of fact and are investigated in the light of the state of the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors must consider what was known and available to skilled persons at the time; the prior art context is essential in applying the negative rules and determining obviousness/invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-only inventions may be patentable (if later proven)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that resides in a theory without reduction to practice at the time the patent was granted may be sustained if the theory afterward proves correct, or when the correctness is self-evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports claims based on theoretical discoveries where later validation or self-evidence shows the theory to be correct; courts have sustained such patents (e.g., Telephone Cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint and sole invention formalities (briefly noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are rules governing joint and sole inventions (e.g., sole patent to one joint inventor is void; joint patent to sole inventor and another is void).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table of contents indicates multiple sections (44–51) treating how joint inventions are made and distinguished, and the consequences when inventorship is misclaimed; proper naming of joint inventors is necessary for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents not void because they include old inventions (combination principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is not necessarily void merely because it covers processes or things that include old inventions; the patentable aspect can be the new combination or improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What matters is whether the combination or improvement is 'invented' (involving inventive faculty) rather than merely the sum of old elements; subcombinations may be patentable.
